runs.text: Memory Fragment: The Bathtub
I remember the bathtub.
Five, maybe seven years old.
Me and my mother curled together, knees to our chests,
Hiding from the pounding at the door.
Cops shouting on the other side, her whispering, “Don’t make a sound.”
The porcelain cold against my back, the water long since drained.
A mother’s breath held, a child’s heartbeat thundering.
I learned early:
Safety is a room you have to earn.
Silence is sometimes survival.
I moved into those same apartments after my daughter was born.
History repeats itself with terrible precision.
The walls unchanged, the tub the same shade of fake porcelain.
Three years of no contact, then my mother moved in with me.
The past walked right back in with her suitcase.
I thought I was building a new life.
But you can’t clean trauma out with bleach and resolve.
I sat on the edge of that same tub,
only now I was the mother,
wondering if I’d break the cycle
or become the echo.
I was fifteen,
and the light in the fridge
felt more honest
than anyone I knew.
Started skipping school
to sit behind the gas station,
watching ants dismantle a candy bar
like they had a plan.
I didn’t.
I had headphones,
a lighter,
and a pocket full of bad ideas.
A trauma backstory.
And too many things
left unsaid at the dinner table.
And once I figured out
no one was coming to save my ass.
I stopped waiting
and just started walking.
Folder said behavior problem and a slew of other things
Fire drills scorched my ears. Buzzing lights. Clicking clock. Frozen hands.
I learned faces and scripts. Passing looked like safety.
Labels rotated: BPD, bipolar, oppositional. None fit.
Years later: autistic, plus ADD. The map appears.
Masking has a name. Burnout has a pattern.
I redesign the room. Fewer inputs. More deep work.
Recovery is scheduled. Passing is optional.
Not broken. Reclassified. I keep the map.

pieces.title: The Refrigerator Was Full of Names

runs.text: I opened the fridge, and it hummed like a familiar hymn.
Inside there were jars, each labeled with a name I forgot to grieve.
Aunt Vicky.
The girl from 3rd grade who let me copy her spelling test.
That version of me who used to pray at red lights.
I touched one jar.
It pulsed with life and then said, “You left me in the year you learned to lie.”
In the freezer, I found a snow globe.
When I shook it,
the snow fell in slow motion,
and inside,
a younger me stood still,
mouth wide open,
never finishing the sentence.
I closed the door.
The light stayed on.
I heard a whisper:
“Memory is perishable. Grief is frostbitten. Hunger is sacred.”
And then I woke up hungry
for names.
I was fourteen.

Home was a place with rules and linoleum floors, not family. When my mom and grandmother came to visit, they brought a small version of love that could fit inside a few shopping bags. A radio. A stack of CDs. Bath and Body Works sprays that smelled like fruit I had never tasted. New clothes. A large stuffed dog. And my grandmother’s quilt, the one I had traced with my finger as a child. It carried the weight of hands that sewed to keep people warm.

I came back from school one afternoon and found wreckage. The girls in my unit had been bored, or angry, or both. The CDs were snapped like brittle cookies. The radio’s antenna bent and jammed. The sprays emptied into the weave of the quilt until it bled sweet chemical air. The stuffed dog was mutilated and paraded around the halls as a joke that aimed to humiliate me.

They told staff I did it to myself. They said I threw a fit and smashed my own things. They spoke quickly and in chorus. I stood there with the quilt dripping perfume and the dog in pieces and the music broken in my hands. Staff nodded at their version, wrote notes, told me to calm down.

I learned something that day. Truth is not loud enough on its own. You need witnesses or proof or power. I had none. I had a ruined quilt, a defaced toy, and the smell of tropical fruit that would not leave the room.

I folded what remained, pressed it flat, and pretended not to care. That is how you survive in places that do not believe you. You make your face still. You pick up what can be carried. You tell yourself a different ending and wait for it to come true.
I was fourteen. I kept the quilt anyway.
